claim: Neuronal KCNQ channels mediate the M-current, a key regulator of membrane excitability in the central and peripheral nervous systems.
source: Neuronal KCNQ channels mediate the M-current, a key regulator of membrane excitability in the central and peripheral nervous systems.

source: Mutations in KCNQ2 channels cause severe neurodevelopmental disorders, including epileptic encephalopathies.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a cryo-EM structure study.

claim: The S5–S6 of the four subunits form a centrally located potassium selective pore that is flanked by the four voltage-sensing domains (VSDs; S1–S4; Long et al., 2005).
source: The S5–S6 of the four subunits form a centrally located potassium selective pore that is flanked by the four voltage- sensing domains (VSDs; S1–S4; Long et al., 2005)

claim: The C-terminal end of the S6 segments forms the gate (Long et al., 2005; del Camino and Yellen, 2001).

claim: The fourth transmembrane segment contains several highly conserved positively charged amino acid residues that move in response to changes in membrane voltages that function as the voltage sensor (Mannuzzu et al., 1996; Larsson et al., 1996; Seoh et al., 1996; Aggarwal and MacKinnon, 1996).

claim: Kv channel opening can occur either after all four S4 have been activated (Zagotta et al., 1994), or alternatively through independent activation of each S4 (Horrigan et al., 1999).

source: We find that two epilepsy-associated mutations cause shifts in the voltage dependence of channel opening by two different mechanisms, with the R198Q mutation shifting S4 movement while the R214W mutation uncoupling VSD and channel opening.
evidence: This claim is supported by VCF data on R198Q and R214W mutations shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cysteine accessibility data suggests that a stretch of 8–9 amino acids (~193 to 200–201), about half of the 17–19 residues forming the S4, moves from a membrane-buried position in the resting state to the extracellular solution during activation gating.
source: Our cysteine accessibility data suggests that a stretch of 8–9 amino acids (~193 to 200–201), about half of the 17–19 residues forming the S4(21), moves from a membrane-buried position in the resting state to the extracellular solution during activation gating.
evidence: This claim is supported by cysteine accessibility data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In a previous study, the first and second positively charged residues of S4 (R198 and R201) were assumed to interact with the first and second counter-charge residues (E130 and E140) in the S2 segment in the closed-resting state.
source: Previously, mutagenesis and disulfide crosslinking of substituted cysteines or metal-ion bridge experiments inferred putative closed-resting states of S4 of KCNQ2 channels (Gourgy-Hacohen et al., 2014). In this study, the first and second positively charged residues of S4 (R198 and R201) were assumed to interact with the first and second counter-charge residues (E130 and E140) in the S2 segment.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of KCNQ2 channels (Li et al., 2021b; PDB:7CR0) revealed the snapshot of the channel in its activated (S4 up) state and the pore in the closed state.
source: More recently, the cryo-EM structure of KCNQ2 channels (Li et al., 2021b; PDB:7CR0) revealed the snapshot of the channel in its activated (S4 up) state and the pore in the closed state.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a cryo-EM structure study.

claim: The cryo-EM structure shows that R198 and R201 have moved about three helical turns outward (upward) from F137 into a position close to or within the extracellular space (Li et al., 2021b).
source: This structure shows that R198 and R201 have moved about three helical turns outward (upward) from F137 into a position close to or within the extracellular space (Li et al., 2021b; Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a cryo-EM structure study and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: The direct measurement of gating charge movement during channel gating (gating current measurements) has not been resolved in KCNQ2 channels (nor in KCNQ3).
source: To date, the direct measurement of gating charge movement during channel gating (gating current measurements) has not been resolved in KCNQ2 channels (nor in KCNQ3).
evidence: This is a statement of fact about the current state of research on KCNQ2 channels.

claim: The VCF signals of the F192C mutant represent a valuable tool to study voltage sensing in human KCNQ2 channels.
source: Therefore, the VCF signals of the F192C mutant reported here represent a valuable tool to study voltage sensing in human KCNQ2 channels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the VCF data presented in the study.

claim: Both labeled and unlabeled F192C mutants alter the gating properties of KCNQ2 channels.
source: Our study reveals, however, that both labeled and unlabeled F192C mutants alter the gating properties of KCNQ2 channels (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The S3–S4 loop is highly sensitive to both mutations and dye-conjugations, with some mutants (and labeled conjugates) generating large shifts of the G(V) relation and accelerating the time course of current activation compared to wt-channels.
source: Our results show that the S3–S4 loop is highly sensitive to both mutations and dye-conjugations, with some mutants (and labeled conjugates) generating large shifts of the G(V) relation and accelerating the time course of current activation compared to wt-channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Similar G(V) shifts of about ~ –10 to –30 mV upon Alexa-488 maleimide labeling have been previously reported in this region for other Kv channels, including KCNQ1(35), KCNQ3(40), BK (Savalli et al., 2006), and Kv1.5 (Vaid et al., 2008).
source: While not optimal, this is not surprising because similar G(V) shifts of about ~ –10 to –30 mV upon Alexa-488 maleimide labeling have been previously reported in this region for other Kv channels, including KCNQ1(35), KCNQ3(40), BK (Savalli et al., 2006), and Kv1.5 (Vaid et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on other Kv channels.

claim: Tethering the dyes Alexa/Dylight to F192C in KCNQ2 channels could interfere with S4 such that labeled F192C might prevent complete S4 deactivation or could help stabilize the activated (or help destabilize the resting) conformation of the S4.
source: We did not explore these effects any further, but it may be possible that tethering the dyes Alexa/Dylight to F192C in KCNQ2 channels could interfere with S4 such that labeled F192C might prevent complete S4 deactivation or could help stabilize the activated (or help destabilize the resting) conformation of the S4, hence shifting the voltage dependence to hyperpolarizing voltages and promoting a faster channel opening.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed effects of dye labeling on F192C channels.

claim: VCF data shows that both the steady-state voltage dependence and the time course of S4 transitions of fluorescent-labeled KCNQ2 channels closely follow those of the ionic currents, which have virtually no delay and no sigmoidal time course.
source: Our VCF data shows that both the steady-state voltage dependence and the time course of S4 transitions of fluorescent-labeled KCNQ2 channels closely follow those of the ionic currents, which have virtually no delay and no sigmoidal time course.
evidence: This claim is supported by VCF data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The close correlations in time and voltage dependence of fluorescence and current of KCNQ2 channels resemble the one-to-one relationship between S4 movement and channel opening reported in KCNQ1 (without KCNE1) (Osteen et al., 2012).
source: The close correlations in time and voltage dependence of fluorescence and current of KCNQ2 channels resemble the one-to-one relationship between S4 movement and channel opening reported in KCNQ1 (without KCNE1) (Osteen et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim compares the current findings to prior research on KCNQ1, supported by a citation.

claim: VCF on linked concatemers of KCNQ1 subunits showed that all four voltage sensors can move independently and channel opening can proceed from individual voltage sensor movements (Osteen et al., 2012).
source: VCF on linked concatemers of KCNQ1 subunits showed that all four voltage sensors can move independently and channel opening can proceed from individual voltage sensor movements (Osteen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on KCNQ1.

claim: S4 does not necessarily require independent conformational changes in all four KCNQ2 subunits before channel opening, as shown for classical voltage-gated K+ channels (Hodgkin and Huxley, 1990), but this needs to be further tested in linked-subunit experiments.
source: These findings indicate that S4 does not necessarily require independent conformational changes in all four KCNQ2 subunits before channel opening, as shown for classical voltage-gated K+ channels (Hodgkin and Huxley, 1990), but this needs to be further tested in linked-subunit experiments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the VCF data and comparison to KCNQ1, with a note that further testing is needed.

claim: In KCNQ4 channels, the S4 moves (measured by gating current) much faster than the rate of activation (ionic current), as if the S4 movement was poorly coupled to opening/closing (Miceli et al., 2012).
source: In KCNQ4 channels, in contrast to KCNQ2, the S4 moves (measured by gating current) much faster than the rate of activation (ionic current), as if the S4 movement was poorly coupled to opening/closing (Miceli et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on KCNQ4.

claim: The gating scheme of KCNQ4 resembles that of the uncoupling R214W mutation, whose S4 movement clearly precedes ionic current.
source: Indeed, the gating scheme of KCNQ4 resembles that of the uncoupling R214W mutation (discussed below), whose S4 movement clearly precedes ionic current (Figure 5D–D').
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing KCNQ4 gating to the R214W mutation data shown in Figure 5D-D'.

claim: Besides the well-characterized KCNQ2/3 and KCNQ3/5 heteromeric channels found in the brain, KCNQ2 not only forms multimeric assemblies with KCNQ5 in vivo, but intriguingly, is able to form part of a more diverse KCNQ2/3/5 heteromeric complex (Soh et al., 2022).
source: For instance, besides the well-characterized KCNQ2/3 and KCNQ3/5 heteromeric channels found in the brain, a recent report shows that KCNQ2 not only forms multimeric assemblies with KCNQ5 in vivo, but intriguingly, is able to form part of a more diverse KCNQ2/3/5 heteromeric complex (Soh et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: The R198Q mutation in KCNQ2 channels causes infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia and encephalopathy associated with severe developmental delay (Millichap et al., 2017).
source: The R198Q mutation in KCNQ2 channels causes infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia and encephalopathy associated with severe developmental delay (Millichap et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior clinical research.

claim: Compared to KCNQ2*, KCNQ2*-R198Q channels display left-shifted G(V) and F(V) curves.
source: Compared to KCNQ2*, KCNQ2*-R198Q channels display left-shifted G(V) and F(V) curves.
evidence: This claim is supported by VCF data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: KCNQ2*-R198Q channels exhibit fluorescence signals and ionic currents that closely overlap in terms of their time courses and voltage dependence of activation.
source: In addition, KCNQ2*-R198Q channels exhibit fluorescence signals and ionic currents that closely overlap in terms of their time courses and voltage dependence of activation (Figure 5B–B' and C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,E, red).
evidence: This claim is supported by VCF data shown in Figure 5B-B', C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, E.

claim: Fluorescence data from the epilepsy-associated mutation R214W shows a marked separation between the G(V) and F(V) and a faster fluorescence time course compared to the ionic current time course.
source: Conversely, fluorescence data from the epilepsy-associated mutation R214W shows a marked separation between the G(V) and F(V) and a faster fluorescence time course compared to the ionic current time course (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1, brown)
evidence: This claim is supported by VCF data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: R214W changes the VSD-PD coupling of KCNQ2.
source: suggesting that R214W changes the VSD-PD coupling of KCNQ2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the VCF data showing separation between F(V) and G(V) for R214W.

claim: KCNQ2*-R214W fluorescence signals do not show a second fluorescence component associated with channel opening.
source: Unlike the ILT mutation in the Shaker K+ channels, in which pore opening is dissociated from the first VSD activation but coupled to the second (Pathak et al., 2005), KCNQ2*-R214W fluorescence signals do not show a second fluorescence component associated with channel opening.
evidence: This is an observation from the VCF data on R214W channels, compared to prior research on Shaker channels.

claim: The R214W and the ILT mutants may decouple VSD-PD through different mechanisms, or alternatively through similar mechanisms but the labeled F192C is unable to resolve the late component of gating charge movement (fluorescence) associated with pore opening.
source: This suggests that the R214W and the ILT mutants decouple VSD-PD through different mechanisms, or alternatively through similar mechanisms but our labeled F192C is unable to resolve the late component of gating charge movement (fluorescence) associated with pore opening.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the VCF data on R214W compared to the ILT mutation.

claim: The F351A mutation in KCNQ1 separated F(V) from G(V) (Osteen et al., 2010a), similar to what is seen with the R214W variant in KCNQ2.
source: Moreover, previous studies in the related KCNQ1 channel showed that the F351A mutation separated F(V) from G(V) (Osteen et al., 2010a), similar to what is seen with the R214W variant in KCNQ2.
evidence: This claim compares the current findings to prior research on KCNQ1, supported by a citation.

claim: It was postulated that KCNQ1-F351 may couple S4 to pore opening possibly through a physical interaction of F351 with residues within the S4–S5 linker such that point mutations like F351A would alter the VSD-PD interactions (Osteen et al., 2010a; Zaydman et al., 2014; Taylor et al., 2020).
source: Mechanistically, it was postulated that KCNQ1-F351 may couple S4 to pore opening possibly through a physical interaction of F351 with residues within the S4–S5 linker such that point mutations like F351A would alter the VSD-PD interactions, suggesting that F351A eliminates the intermediate open state (Osteen et al., 2010a; Zaydman et al., 2014; Taylor et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on KCNQ1.

claim: Unlike the F351 residue that is localized in the S6 helix (PD) pointing toward the S4–S5 linker of KCNQ1 channels (Sun and MacKinnon, 2020), the R214 residue of KCNQ2 lies in the loop region that connects the S4 to the S4–S5 linker (Li et al., 2021b).
source: However, unlike the F351 residue that is localized in the S6 helix (PD) pointing toward the S4–S5 linker of KCNQ1 channels (Sun and MacKinnon, 2020), the R214 residue of KCNQ2 lies in the loop region that connects the S4 to the S4–S5 linker (Li et al., 2021b; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: F351A and R214W may decouple VSD-PD through different mechanisms.
source: as if F351A and R214W may also decouple VSD-PD through different mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different structural locations of F351 and R214.

claim: The cryo-EM structures of KCNQ1 and KCNQ4 show PIP2 bound to these channels close to the S4/S4–S5 interface, in a positively charged pocket.
source: The cryo-EM structures of KCNQ1 and KCNQ4 show PIP2 bound to these channels close to the S4/S4–S5 interface, in a positively charged pocket.
evidence: This claim is based on structural information from cryo-EM studies of KCNQ1 and KCNQ4.

claim: Residue R214 in KCNQ2 lies very close to PIP2, suggesting that R214 in the KCNQ2 channel could form part of the positively charged pocket that coordinates PIP2 binding.
source: Superimposing the KCNQ2 structure (Long et al., 2005) with the homologous structure of KCNQ1 bound to PIP2(55) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), we noted that residue R214 lies very close to PIP2, suggesting that R214 in the KCNQ2 channel could form part of the positively charged pocket that coordinates PIP2 binding (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural superimposition shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Previous studies in KCNQ1 and KCNQ3 channels have shown that PIP2 directly affects the VSD-PD coupling (Kim et al., 2017; Zaydman et al., 2013).
source: Previous studies in KCNQ1 and KCNQ3 channels have shown that PIP2 directly affects the VSD-PD coupling (Kim et al., 2017; Zaydman et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In KCNQ2, PIP2 may act like a molecular 'glue' that tightly ties the loop connecting S4 and S4–S5 linker such that during depolarization, the S4 movement effectively pulls S4–S5 away from the pore domain to activate potassium conductance.
source: Based on our VCF results (Figure 5D and E), which suggest that the R214W mutant dissociates S4 movement from channel opening, we hypothesize that the positive charge of residue R214 is crucial for PIP2 binding. We propose that in KCNQ2, PIP2 may act like a molecular 'glue' that tightly ties the loop connecting S4 and S4–S5 linker such that during depolarization, the S4 movement effectively pulls S4–S5 away from the pore domain to activate potassium conductance.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the VCF data and structural considerations.

claim: Charge-neutralizing mutations like the R214W variant would affect PIP2 binding and, thereby, weaken the VSD-PD coupling.
source: Therefore, charge-neutralizing mutations like the R214W variant, would affect PIP2 binding and, thereby, weaken the VSD-PD coupling.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the proposed role of R214 in PIP2 binding.

claim: Previous studies on KCNQ2 channels bearing the charge neutralizing mutations, R214Q or R214W, found that the loss of the positive charge, and not changes in residue size, was the main functional effect of these disease-associated mutations (Miceli et al., 2008).
source: Supporting this idea, previous studies on KCNQ2 channels bearing the charge neutralizing mutations, R214Q or R214W, found that the loss of the positive charge, and not changes in residue size, was the main functional effect of these disease-associated mutations as both smaller hydrophilic glutamine and bulkier aromatic tryptophan residues at position 214 favored the resting conformation of S4 and, as such, promoted more channel closure (Miceli et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Understanding the impact of human mutations in key regions of the channel, such as the VSD and the pore, will facilitate the prediction of compounds that most effectively restore functionality to specific channel mutations while minimizing potential off-target effects.
source: Understanding the impact of human mutations in key regions of the channel, such as the VSD and the pore, will facilitate the prediction of compounds that most effectively restore functionality to specific channel mutations while minimizing potential off-target effects.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential implications of the research for drug development.

claim: Small-molecule modulators of KCNQ2 channels have been identified, including the pore opener retigabine (Maljevic and Lerche, 2014; Brodie et al., 2010; Wuttke and Lerche, 2006) and the VSD-targeting ICA family of compounds (Wulff et al., 2009; Wickenden et al., 2008; Roeloffs et al., 2008).
source: Small-molecule modulators of KCNQ2 channels have been identified, including the pore opener retigabine (Maljevic and Lerche, 2014; Brodie et al., 2010; Wuttke and Lerche, 2006) and the VSD-targeting ICA family of compounds (Wulff et al., 2009; Wickenden et al., 2008; Roeloffs et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on KCNQ2 modulators.

claim: Retigabine exhibits poor specificity between KCNQ channel subunits (except for KCNQ1) possibly due to its binding to the S5 segment of the pore (Wuttke et al., 2005).
source: Retigabine exhibits poor specificity between KCNQ channel subunits (except for KCNQ1) possibly due to its binding to the S5 segment of the pore (Wuttke et al., 2005), which in contrast to the highly diverse VSD region, shows a more conserved sequence among Kv channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on retigabine.

claim: Pore openers like retigabine, which cause a hyperpolarizing shift in the voltage dependence of activation, might seem like a suitable choice to effectively target VSD-PD uncoupling mutations like R214W, but off-target effects on other KCNQ subunits would need to be considered.
source: Pore openers like retigabine, which cause a hyperpolarizing shift in the voltage dependence of activation, might seem like a suitable choice to effectively target VSD-PD uncoupling mutations like R214W, but off-target effects on other KCNQ subunits would need to be considered.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic strategies.

claim: ICA-like compounds act on the VSD, a less conserved region compared to the pore, presumably allowing ICA to distinguish between KCNQ subunits (Wickenden et al., 2008; Padilla et al., 2009).
source: Unlike retigabine, ICA-like compounds act on the VSD, a less conserved region compared to the pore, presumably allowing ICA to distinguish between KCNQ subunits (Wickenden et al., 2008; Padilla et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on ICA compounds.

claim: ICA-like compounds (but in a manner that rightward shifts its voltage dependence) would be more effective to target mutations like R198Q that disturb the VSD.
source: Therefore, ICA-like compounds (but in a manner that rightward shifts its voltage dependence) would be more effective to target mutations like R198Q that disturb the VSD.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic strategies based on the findings.

claim: The perfusion system quickly delivers a 5 s pulse of MTSET to the external surface of oocytes, ensuring perfusion of MTSET only at the indicated voltage.
source: Note that the perfusion system quickly delivers a 5 s pulse of MTSET to the external surface of oocytes. This ensures perfusion of MTSET only at the indicated voltage as shown by the time course of solution exchange from 100 mM NaCl to 100 mM KCl (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the solution exchange experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The rate of MTSET modification of R198C channels is kopen = 3230 ± 3.8 M–1 s–1 (n=8) in the open state.
source: The fitted second-order rate constant in the open state protocol is shown in red. kopen = 3230 ± 3.8 M–1 s–1 (n=8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.
